title: Network Security
summary: How networks are attacked and defended: eavesdropping, spoofing, MITM and DDoS, firewalls and segmentation, TLS 1.3 in depth, VPNs and tunnels, Wi-Fi security, and detecting intruders with IDS, packet captures and flow logs.

lessons.title: Privacy and forged packet identities
lessons.summary: An address in a packet is a claim, not cryptographic proof of the sender.
lessons.body:
Basic IPv4, ARP, UDP and traditional DNS do not by themselves cryptographically authenticate every sender or encrypt application data. Checksums detect some accidental corruption, but do not prove identity. Security extensions and deployment controls can add protections.

Missing authentication and encryption enable several important network attacks. These threat units sort attacks into five families. For each one, ask two questions: **what security property does it break**, and **what is the standard defence**?

The classic properties are often summarised as **CIA**:

| Property | Meaning | Broken by |
|---|---|---|
| Confidentiality | Only the intended party reads it | Eavesdropping |
| Integrity | Nobody alters it undetected | MITM, injection |
| Authenticity | It came from who it claims | Spoofing, replay |
| Availability | The service stays up | DoS / DDoS |

(Strictly, CIA is confidentiality, integrity and availability; authenticity is usually grouped with integrity. It is listed separately here because so many network attacks target it.)

## Eavesdropping

**Eavesdropping** (passive sniffing) means reading traffic you were not meant to see. The attacker changes nothing, which makes it very hard to detect.

Where can an attacker listen?

- **Shared media.** Wi-Fi is radio: a nearby receiver may capture frames on a monitored channel, subject to signal, interference and radio capabilities. An Ethernet repeater hub repeated received signals onto its other ports, subject to physical-layer error and collision handling.
- **Switched LANs.** A switch normally forwards known unicasts toward the learned destination port, while broadcasts and some unknown traffic are flooded. Exhausting the switch's MAC address table, or ARP poisoning, may expose additional traffic, depending on switch protections and topology.
- **On the path.** Any ISP, transit provider, café router or compromised router between you and the server sees your packets.

Even when the payload is encrypted, **metadata** leaks: source and destination addresses, packet sizes, timing, and often the server's hostname (in DNS queries and the TLS SNI field, covered in the TLS units).

The defence is **encryption in transit**: TLS for application traffic, VPNs for whole networks, WPA2/WPA3 for Wi-Fi. The maths behind the ciphers is covered in the Security & Cryptography subject; here we care about where encryption sits and what it leaves exposed.

## Spoofing

**Spoofing** means forging an identifier. Many packet fields can be written by a sender. Whether a forgery is accepted depends on filtering, cryptographic validation and protocol state.

| What is forged | How | Classic use |
|---|---|---|
| Source IP | Write any value in the header | Reflection DDoS |
| MAC address | Change the NIC setting | Bypass MAC filters |
| ARP reply | Send unsolicited replies | LAN MITM |
| DNS answer | Race the real reply | Redirect a domain |
| Email sender | Set the From header | Phishing |

**IP spoofing** has a catch for the attacker: replies go to the forged address, not to them. So it is mostly useful for one-way attacks where the attacker does not need the answer. That is exactly what reflection attacks need, as covered in the later amplification units.

An off-path attacker who cannot observe replies has an additional obstacle when forging a TCP handshake: the acknowledgment must match the server's initial sequence number plus one in the ordinary no-data handshake. With an unpredictable 32-bit initial sequence number, one blind guess is right only about once in 4.3 billion tries. Predictable sequence numbers once made blind spoofing practical, which is why RFC 6528 recommends unpredictable generation.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a forged sender's name on a letter
> Anyone can write any name in the sender's corner of a letter and post it. The post office delivers it without checking, and any reply goes to the name and address written there, not to the person who really sent it.
>
> **How it maps:** The source address in an IP packet is the written sender's name. Routers forward on the destination and do not prove the source, so replies go to the forged address. That is why spoofing suits one-way floods and reflection, and why a blind attacker cannot see a server's reply.
>
> **Where it stops:** Networks can check sources in ways the post office does not: BCP 38 filtering drops packets whose source is outside the customer's permitted prefixes, and protocols such as TCP and TLS add state or cryptographic proof that a forger must also defeat.

> [!tip] BCP 38: stop spoofing at the source
> RFC 2827 (BCP 38) recommends filtering customer traffic against permitted source prefixes. This blocks spoofing outside those prefixes, but does not by itself stop one host impersonating another inside an allowed prefix. More granular source validation and reflector controls are also useful.

## Key takeaways
- An address in a packet is a claim, not cryptographic proof of the sender.
- Encryption hides protected content but leaves observable metadata.
- BCP 38 filters unauthorised source prefixes; it does not identify every individual sender.

## Further reading
- [RFC 2827 (BCP 38): Network Ingress Filtering](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2827)
- [RFC 6528: Defending against Sequence Number Attacks](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6528)
- [RFC 4987: TCP SYN Flooding Attacks and Common Mitigations](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4987)
- [Man-in-the-middle attack — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man-in-the-middle_attack)

questions.prompt: An attacker passively captures nearby Wi-Fi traffic to try to read another user's data. Which security property is targeted?

options.text: Availability
options.explanation: Nothing is being disrupted: the attacker sends no traffic, so the network keeps working normally.

options.text: Confidentiality
options.explanation: Correct. Passive eavesdropping targets confidentiality. Capturing ciphertext alone does not necessarily reveal application plaintext.

options.text: Integrity
options.explanation: Integrity is broken when data is altered. A passive sniffer changes nothing.

options.text: Authenticity
options.explanation: Authenticity is broken by forging who sent something (spoofing, replay). Listening alone forges nothing.

questions.workedExample:
1. Ask what the attacker *does*: receive frames only.
2. Nothing is changed, so integrity is intact.
3. Nothing is forged, so authenticity is intact.
4. Nothing is slowed down, so availability is intact.
5. The target is secrecy: reading data meant for someone else would violate **confidentiality**. Correctly encrypted ciphertext need not reveal its plaintext.

The defence is encryption in transit (WPA2/WPA3, TLS, a VPN). Even then, metadata such as addresses, sizes and timing still leak.

questions.prompt: For an off-path attacker unable to observe replies to the forged address, why is IP source-address spoofing well suited to reflection DDoS but poor for logging in to a remote server?

options.text: Routers detect and drop most spoofed packets, so only floods get through
options.explanation: Many networks still do not filter spoofed sources (BCP 38 is not universal), so spoofed packets often reach their target. This is not the reason.

options.text: Spoofed packets are always UDP
options.explanation: You can write any source address in any IP packet, TCP included. The protocol is not the limit.

options.text: Replies go to the forged address, so the attacker never sees them; a flood does not need replies, but a login does
options.explanation: Correct. Reflection wants the replies to land on the victim. A login is a two-way conversation, and the attacker cannot see the server's answers.

options.text: Spoofing only works on a local network
options.explanation: IP spoofing works across the internet wherever ingress filtering is missing; it is ARP spoofing that is limited to the LAN.

questions.workedExample:
1. The attacker writes the victim's IP as the source.
2. The server replies to that address, so the reply goes to the victim.
3. For reflection this is the goal: the victim receives the responses.
4. For a login the attacker needs the server's replies (including TCP's SYN-ACK and its 32-bit initial sequence number). They never see them, so they would have to guess, and modern stacks randomise the number.

So spoofing suits one-way attacks.

questions.prompt: An off-path attacker wants to open a complete TCP connection to a server while forging a trusted host's IP address. The server's SYN-ACK goes to the real host, so the attacker never sees it. Which server behaviour would make this blind attack practical?

options.text: A large TCP receive window
options.explanation: The window limits how much data may be in flight once a connection exists. It does not tell the attacker which acknowledgment number completes the handshake.

options.text: Initial sequence numbers that are predictable, for example rising by a fixed step per connection
options.explanation: Correct. The attacker's final ACK must acknowledge the server's initial sequence number plus one. If that number can be predicted, the attacker can complete the handshake without seeing the SYN-ACK. Unpredictable 32-bit values leave only about one chance in 4.3 billion per blind guess.

options.text: Answering SYNs very quickly
options.explanation: Speed changes when the SYN-ACK is sent, not whether the attacker can learn its sequence number. The reply still goes to the forged address.

options.text: Running the service on a high-numbered port instead of a well-known one
options.explanation: The attacker must know the port to send the SYN at all, so the port number is not a secret. It reveals nothing about the server's initial sequence number.

questions.workedExample:
1. Spoofing the source means the server's SYN-ACK, and the initial sequence number (ISN) inside it, goes to the real owner of that address.
2. To finish the handshake the attacker must send an ACK whose acknowledgment number is exactly the server's ISN plus one.
3. Without seeing the SYN-ACK, the attacker must predict or guess that number.
4. If the server picks ISNs unpredictably across 32 bits, a single guess almost never succeeds (about once in 4.3 billion tries).
5. If ISNs follow a pattern, the attacker can predict the next one, and the blind connection becomes practical. This was a real historical attack, and RFC 6528 recommends unpredictable ISN generation for this reason.

The other options change timing, buffering or which port is used, not what the attacker can predict.

lessons.title: Authentication and replay protection
lessons.summary: An encrypted channel to an impostor still exposes data to that impostor.
lessons.body:
A passive observer reads traffic; an active attacker may relay it or resend an earlier valid message. The objective here is to distinguish peer authentication from message freshness.

## Man-in-the-middle

A **man-in-the-middle (MITM)** attacker sits between two parties, relaying and possibly altering traffic while each side believes it is talking directly to the other. An unmitigated MITM can threaten confidentiality, integrity and authentication; correctly authenticated encryption can prevent reading or modifying protected content even when traffic is relayed.

```
 Normal:
 Alice ------------------------> Bank

 MITM:
 Alice ----> Mallory ----> Bank
   "I am the Bank"  "I am Alice"
```

Ways to get in the middle:

- **ARP spoofing** on a LAN: tell the victim "the gateway's IP is at my MAC address".
- **Rogue Wi-Fi access points** ("evil twins", the wireless units).
- **DNS spoofing**: make the domain resolve to the attacker's IP.
- **BGP hijacking**: an unauthorised announcement may redirect traffic in networks that accept and select it.

Encryption alone does not stop MITM. If Alice does a key exchange with Mallory, she has a perfectly encrypted channel to the attacker. What stops MITM is **authentication**: Alice must verify she is talking to the real bank. In TLS that is the certificate check (the TLS units). This is why clicking through a certificate warning is so dangerous.

## Replay

In a **replay attack** the attacker captures a valid message and sends it again later. They do not need to read or change it.

> [!example] A replayed payment
> A client sends an encrypted, signed message: "pay merchant £50". The attacker cannot read it, but captures it and sends it ten more times. If the server only checks the signature, it pays out £550.

The signature is valid every time, because it is the same message. The defence is to make each message usable **once**:

- **Nonces**: include a unique value in the authenticated request; atomically reject reuse in the relevant session or account.
- **Timestamps**: an authenticated timestamp can limit the timestamp validity interval, but a replay inside that window still needs duplicate detection. Clock and expiry rules must be defined.
- **Sequence numbers**: authenticate counters and track accepted values. An ordered channel can require the next counter; an IPsec-style anti-replay window can accept unseen out-of-order packets while rejecting duplicates and packets that are too old. TLS early data has separate replay caveats (the TLS units).

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: numbered cheques
> A bank honours a genuine signed cheque once. If someone photocopies it and presents the copy, the signature still looks right, so the bank relies on something else: it records each cheque number it has paid and refuses a number it has already seen, and it refuses cheques that are too old.
>
> **How it maps:** The signature is message authentication: it proves who wrote the message, not that this copy is new. The cheque number is a nonce or sequence number, the bank's record of paid numbers is the receiver's replay state, and the "too old" rule is a timestamp or window limit.
>
> **Where it stops:** A paper copy can often be told apart from the original, but a replayed network message is bit-for-bit identical. The receiver can only reject it by checking authenticated freshness data against stored state, and that check must be atomic so two copies arriving together cannot both be accepted.

## Key takeaways
- An encrypted channel to an impostor still exposes data to that impostor.
- Preventing replay needs authenticated freshness information and receiver state.
- A timestamp bounds age; duplicate detection handles reuse inside that bound.

## Further reading
- [Replay attack — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Replay_attack)
- [Man-in-the-middle attack — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man-in-the-middle_attack)
- [RFC 4303: IP Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP), anti-replay service](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4303)

questions.prompt: Alice connects to her bank over a link that Mallory controls. Mallory performs a key exchange with Alice and a separate one with the bank, then relays traffic. Both channels use strong encryption. What would have stopped this?

options.text: A longer encryption key
options.explanation: Key length is irrelevant: Alice's channel is perfectly encrypted, just to the wrong party.

options.text: Alice checking that she is really talking to the bank, for example by validating its certificate
options.explanation: Correct. A man-in-the-middle is defeated by authentication. Assuming the trust store and bank credentials are uncompromised, Mallory cannot supply the required name-bound authentication proof, so verification fails.

options.text: Using TCP instead of UDP
options.explanation: The transport protocol does not prove identity. Mallory can relay TCP just as easily.

options.text: Compressing the data before encrypting it
options.explanation: Compression does nothing for identity, and compression before encryption has caused real attacks (CRIME).

questions.workedExample:
1. Encryption gives confidentiality *with whoever you did the key exchange with*.
2. Alice did her key exchange with Mallory, so Mallory can decrypt everything.
3. The missing step is **authentication**: proof that the other end is the bank.
4. In certificate-authenticated TLS, validate the certificate chain and bank name, and verify the server's proof of the corresponding private key. A copied public certificate alone is insufficient.
5. This is why clicking through a certificate warning hands a MITM exactly what they need.

questions.prompt: A client sends a signed message, "transfer £50 to account 1234". An attacker cannot read or alter it but captures it. Assume added freshness fields are authenticated and receiver checks update state atomically. Which measures prevent an identical request from being accepted twice, even within a valid timestamp window? Select all that apply.

options.text: Include a unique nonce the server records and refuses to accept twice
options.explanation: Correct. The second copy carries a nonce the server has already seen, so it is rejected.

options.text: Use a stronger signature algorithm
options.explanation: Incorrect. The replayed message is the genuine message, so any signature verifies. Signature strength is not the problem.

options.text: Include a timestamp and reject messages older than a few seconds
options.explanation: Incorrect as a complete replay defence: the attacker can resend within the accepted time window. A timestamp limits age but still needs authenticated duplicate detection.

options.text: Encrypt the message as well as signing it
options.explanation: Incorrect. The attacker never needed to read it; they resend the encrypted bytes unchanged.

options.text: Include a per-session sequence number that must increase
options.explanation: Correct if the counter is authenticated, scoped to the session and acceptance state is updated atomically. Strictly increasing acceptance rejects the repeated counter; anti-replay-window protocols instead track duplicates while tolerating some reordering.

questions.workedExample:
A duplicate must be distinguishable through authenticated freshness data and receiver state.

| Measure | Identical replay rejected? |
|---|---|
| Recorded authenticated nonce | Yes, including inside the time window |
| Stronger signature alone | No; original signature remains valid |
| Timestamp alone | Only after expiry, not within the window |
| Encryption alone | No; the same protected bytes can be replayed |
| Authenticated increasing session counter | Yes, with atomic acceptance state |

Neither stronger encryption nor a valid signature by itself guarantees freshness.

lessons.title: Which resource does a denial of service exhaust?
lessons.summary: Volumetric, protocol-state and application attacks exhaust different resources.
lessons.body:
Traffic can be authentic and still exhaust a service. Identify the constrained resource before choosing a defence: link capacity, retained state and expensive application work need different controls.

## Denial of service

A **denial-of-service (DoS)** attack stops a service working for its legitimate users. A **distributed** DoS (DDoS) uses many sources, typically a **botnet** of compromised machines. The Mirai botnet of 2016, built from hacked cameras and routers, disrupted DNS resolution at Dyn and access to many customer websites.

DDoS attacks are classified by the resource they exhaust:

| Class | Exhausts | Measured in | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Volumetric | Link bandwidth | bits/s | UDP reflection |
| Protocol | State tables | packets/s | SYN flood |
| Application | Server CPU / app | requests/s | HTTP flood |

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: three ways to stop a restaurant serving
> A restaurant can be stopped in three different ways. A traffic jam can block the only road in, so no customers arrive. Pranksters can book every table and never turn up, so real diners are turned away while the tables sit empty. Or a few customers can order the most elaborate dishes again and again, so the kitchen falls behind.
>
> **How it maps:** The road is link bandwidth (volumetric attacks), the reserved tables are connection state such as half-open TCP entries (protocol attacks), and the overworked kitchen is application CPU or worker threads (application-layer attacks). Each needs its own fix: a wider road or diversion upstream, a booking rule that holds no table until the guest confirms (SYN cookies), or limits and caching in the kitchen.
>
> **Where it stops:** Real attacks often mix types, and network traffic can be forged in ways diners cannot: thousands of sources may be spoofed or hijacked devices. A restaurant also cannot clone itself across the world the way an anycast scrubbing network spreads load.

### Volumetric

Fill the victim's pipe with more traffic than it can carry. If the link is 10 Gbps and 50 Gbps arrives, legitimate packets are dropped upstream, before your servers ever see them. You cannot filter your way out on your own equipment; mitigation must happen upstream, at your ISP or a scrubbing service (Cloudflare, Akamai, AWS Shield) with sufficient capacity and filtering for the particular attack. Cloudflare reported a record 31.4 Tbps attack, lasting about 35 seconds, in its [2025 Q4 report](https://blog.cloudflare.com/ddos-threat-report-2025-q4/) (published February 2026, and still its largest reported figure as of October 2026); this is a provider-reported measurement, not a limit on future attacks.

### Protocol

Exhaust a stateful resource with relatively little bandwidth. The classic is the **SYN flood**: send many TCP SYNs (often with spoofed sources) and never complete the handshake. Each one occupies a slot in the server's half-open connection queue until it times out.

The standard defence is **SYN cookies**. For a SYN handled with a cookie, the server avoids retaining a per-request half-open connection entry. It encodes limited information in the SYN-ACK's initial sequence number; the client's acknowledgment is that number plus one. The server validates the cookie and reconstructs connection state. Shared keys, counters and transient packet processing still exist. Firewalls and load balancers with connection tables are also protocol-attack targets.

### Application layer

Send requests that look legitimate but are expensive: searches, logins, uncached pages. A few thousand requests per second hitting a slow database query can do more damage than gigabits of junk.

**Slowloris** is the low-and-slow variant: open many HTTP connections and send headers one byte at a time, never finishing. Thread-per-connection servers (classic Apache) run out of workers. Defences include rate limiting, CAPTCHAs or challenges, caching, and event-driven servers or reverse proxies with short deadlines for receiving headers.

## Key takeaways
- Volumetric, protocol-state and application attacks exhaust different resources.
- A SYN handled by a cookie avoids a retained per-request half-open entry.
- A saturated access link needs mitigation before that link.

## Further reading
- [RFC 4987: TCP SYN Flooding Attacks and Common Mitigations](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4987)
- [Understanding the Mirai Botnet (USENIX Security 2017)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity17/technical-sessions/presentation/antonakakis)
- [Slowloris (computer security) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slowloris_(computer_security))

questions.prompt: For an incoming SYN that the server handles using a SYN cookie, what changes compared with retaining a conventional half-open queue entry?

options.text: It drops every SYN from an address it has not seen before
options.explanation: That would block every new legitimate client. Cookies allow eligible new attempts without retaining a half-open entry; filtering and capacity limits may still drop SYNs.

options.text: It allocates a larger half-open queue
options.explanation: A bigger queue only delays exhaustion. SYN cookies remove the need for a queue entry altogether.

options.text: It requires the client to solve a proof-of-work puzzle
options.explanation: That is a different idea (client puzzles). TCP clients need no changes for SYN cookies.

options.text: It avoids a per-request half-open entry and puts a verifiable cookie in the SYN-ACK initial sequence number
options.explanation: Correct. The acknowledgment contains cookie + 1. After validation the server can reconstruct connection state; this saves half-open entries but does not eliminate packet-processing costs.

questions.workedExample:
1. Normal TCP: on SYN, store a half-open entry and send a SYN-ACK. Each entry waits for an ACK until timeout.
2. Spoofed SYNs never send that ACK, so entries pile up until the queue is full.
3. For a cookie-handled SYN the server does not retain a per-request half-open entry. It picks its ISN as a keyed hash of the 4-tuple plus a time counter and an encoded MSS.
4. When the client's ACK arrives, its acknowledgment number should be the cookie plus one, because the server's SYN uses up one sequence number, so the handshake ACK acknowledges the initial sequence number plus one. The server subtracts one to recover the cookie and checks the hash. If it checks out, the server recreates the connection state.
5. Cost: some TCP options are lost or have to be squeezed into the cookie. On Linux, the setting `tcp_syncookies=1` uses cookies only when the SYN queue overflows; value 2 makes the server use cookies for every SYN.

questions.prompt: Your data centre has a 10 Gbps internet link. A 40 Gbps UDP reflection attack begins. Why can't your own edge firewall solve this, however good its rules are?

options.text: Firewalls cannot filter UDP
options.explanation: Firewalls filter UDP routinely. The rules are not the problem.

options.text: The link is already saturated before traffic reaches the firewall, so legitimate packets are dropped upstream
options.explanation: Correct. 40 Gbps cannot fit down a 10 Gbps pipe. The ISP's router drops the excess, good and bad alike, before your firewall sees it. Mitigation must happen upstream.

options.text: Reflection traffic comes from legitimate servers, so firewalls must accept it
options.explanation: You could block the reflectors' source port, but it would not matter: the pipe is full before the firewall can drop anything.

options.text: Firewalls only inspect TCP handshakes
options.explanation: Stateful firewalls track UDP flows too; this misunderstands what they do.

questions.workedExample:
1. Volumetric attacks exhaust **bandwidth**, measured in bits per second.
2. Capacity in: 10 Gbps. Offered load: 40 Gbps (plus your normal traffic).
3. The bottleneck is the provider's router feeding your link. With a sustained 40 Gbps offered load and a 10 Gbps output, queues cannot absorb the excess indefinitely. Which packets are dropped depends on scheduling and upstream filtering; it is not necessarily three quarters of each traffic class.
4. Your firewall can drop attack packets, but only the ones that already made it through.
5. Fix: upstream filtering at the ISP, a scrubbing service, or anycast spreading the load across many sites with far more capacity.

questions.prompt: A thread-per-connection web server has 400 worker threads. An attacker on a home connection opens 400 connections and sends one header line on each every 10 seconds, never finishing the request. Real users get no response. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Buy a bigger internet link
options.explanation: The attack uses almost no bandwidth, so more bandwidth changes nothing.

options.text: Block UDP at the firewall
options.explanation: This is an HTTP attack over TCP; UDP filtering is irrelevant.

options.text: Enable SYN cookies
options.explanation: The handshakes complete normally. SYN cookies protect the half-open queue, not worker threads stuck on completed connections.

options.text: Put an event-driven reverse proxy in front with a short timeout for receiving complete headers
options.explanation: Correct. This is Slowloris. An event-driven proxy holds thousands of idle connections cheaply, and a header timeout drops the dribbling ones, so the workers only see complete requests.

questions.workedExample:
1. Classify: low bandwidth, completed TCP handshakes, incomplete HTTP requests. That is **Slowloris**, an application-layer attack.
2. The resource exhausted is worker threads: 400 connections each holding a thread.
3. Each connection stays just inside the server's idle timeout by sending a line every 10 s.
4. Fixes that target the resource:
   - Event-driven servers or proxies (nginx, HAProxy) that do not tie a thread to a connection.
   - A total deadline for receiving headers.
   - Per-IP connection limits.

lessons.title: Reflection and amplification budgets
lessons.summary: Reflection directs replies to a forged victim address.
lessons.body:
Source-address spoofing becomes a bandwidth problem when public UDP servers send large replies to small requests. This unit traces that path and explains what limits how big the resulting flood can get.

## Amplification attacks

One important family of volumetric attacks combines spoofing with **reflection and amplification**:

```
 Attacker            Reflectors       Victim
   |  small query,       |               |
   |  src = victim IP    |               |
   |-------------------->|               |
   |                     | big response  |
   |                     |-------------->|
   |                     |  (x N)        |
```

1. The attacker sends a small UDP request to a public server (DNS resolver, NTP server, memcached instance), with the **source IP forged as the victim's**.
2. The server replies, to the victim, with a much larger response.
3. Thousands of reflectors do the same, all aiming at the victim.

UDP is used because there is no handshake to verify the source. The reflectors are innocent and the victim sees traffic from thousands of legitimate servers, which is hard to block.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: free catalogues sent to someone else's address
> Imagine posting thousands of one-line postcards to mail-order firms, each asking for their heaviest free catalogue and each giving your victim's address. Every firm innocently posts a catalogue, and the victim's doormat is buried under mail they never asked for.
>
> **How it maps:** The postcard is the small spoofed request, the firms are the reflectors, the forged address is the victim's IP in the source field, and the catalogue's weight compared with the postcard is the amplification factor. The firms cannot easily tell the request was forged, and the victim cannot simply refuse mail from well-known firms.
>
> **Where it stops:** Network reflection happens in milliseconds and at enormous scale, and each request costs the attacker almost nothing. Reflectors are limited by their own links and rate limits in a way the analogy hides, and networks can drop forged-source packets at the sender's ISP (BCP 38), which has no postal equivalent.

### The amplification factor

To compare reflectors, you need one number: how many bytes come back for every byte the attacker sends. That ratio is the **bandwidth amplification factor (BAF)**:

```formula essential
BAF = B_resp / B_req
where
BAF: the bandwidth amplification factor, a plain ratio with no unit; 1 means no amplification
B_resp: the size of the response the reflector sends to the victim, in bytes (B)
B_req: the size of the request the attacker sends to the reflector, in bytes (B)
B: bytes; one byte is 8 bits
In words: the amplification factor is how many times bigger the reflected response is than the spoofed request that triggered it.
```

For example, a 40-byte request that triggers a 1,400-byte response has a payload BAF of 35. The ratio depends on which bytes you count (payload only, or headers too; the next unit compares them) and on the particular query and server, so published figures are measurements, not constants.

The following historical examples use UDP-payload ratios. Rossow's 2014 measurements report sample means for particular queries and servers; GitHub's 2018 incident report cites an upper memcached example. They are not fixed protocol constants or current guarantees:

| Protocol | Approx. BAF |
|---|---|
| DNS | 28.7 (open resolvers), 54.6 (authoritative servers) |
| SSDP | 30.8 |
| NTP (monlist) | 556.9 |
| CharGEN | 358.8 |
| Memcached | Up to 51,000 in the cited 2018 report |

### How big can the flood get?

In an idealised model, the traffic arriving at the victim is the attackers' combined sending rate multiplied by the BAF. For example, 2,000 bots each sending 5 Mbps give 10 Gbps of requests; reflected through DNS servers with a BAF of about 50 (a round figure near the table's authoritative-server measurement), that is up to about 500 Gbps at the victim.

That figure is a ceiling, not a prediction. It assumes every request reaches a reflector, every reflector answers, and nothing is lost. Real attacks fall short because:

- **Reflectors have their own limits.** Each reflector's uplink, CPU and any response rate limiting cap what it can send, however many requests arrive.
- **Requests and replies are lost** along congested paths.
- **The BAF varies** by query and server, and the attacker may not find enough high-amplification reflectors.

Through exposed memcached servers even a 1 Gbps attacker could, in principle, generate tens of Tbps (terabits per second; 1 Tbps = 1,000 Gbps); in practice the reflectors' own links capped it. In 2018 GitHub absorbed a 1.35 Tbps memcached attack.

The practical lesson is that the BAF tells you which services are dangerous to leave exposed, while the reflectors' total capacity and the attacker's sending rate decide how large an attack actually gets.

## Key takeaways
- Reflection directs replies to a forged victim address.
- Specify which bytes a bandwidth amplification factor counts.
- Multiplying sending rate by BAF gives a ceiling that assumes sufficient reflector capacity and no loss.

## Further reading
- [UDP-Based Amplification Attacks — CISA](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2014/01/17/udp-based-amplification-attacks)
- [Amplification Hell: Revisiting Network Protocols for DDoS Abuse (NDSS 2014)](https://www.ndss-symposium.org/ndss2014/programme/amplification-hell-revisiting-network-protocols-ddos-abuse/)
- [February 28th DDoS incident report — GitHub blog](https://github.blog/news-insights/company-news/ddos-incident-report/)

questions.prompt: An analyst multiplies a botnet's combined upload rate by the reflectors' bandwidth amplification factor (BAF) and predicts 500 Gbps at the victim. The victim actually measures about 80 Gbps of reflected traffic. Which explanation is most consistent with how amplification works?

options.text: The BAF must have been measured wrongly, because rate times BAF is exact
options.explanation: Rate times BAF is an idealised ceiling. It assumes every request reaches a reflector, every reflector answers and nothing is lost, so a lower real figure does not show the BAF was wrong.

options.text: The reflectors' own uplinks, CPU and response rate limits capped how much they could send, and some requests and replies were lost
options.explanation: Correct. Each reflector can send only what its link and configuration allow, however many spoofed requests arrive, and congested paths drop packets. These limits make the real flood smaller than the ideal product.

options.text: Spoofed requests are always dropped by the attacker's ISP
options.explanation: If they were always dropped there would be no reflected traffic at all. BCP 38 filtering is not universal, which is why reflection attacks still work.

options.text: Amplification only applies to TCP, so UDP reflectors do not amplify
options.explanation: It is the other way round: UDP reflection works because there is no handshake to verify the source address. The classic amplifiers (DNS, NTP, memcached) are UDP services.

questions.workedExample:
1. The model 'combined upload × BAF' answers: how much could arrive if everything went perfectly?
2. It silently assumes enough reflectors, each with spare capacity, answering every request, with no loss on the way.
3. In practice each reflector's uplink and rate limiting cap its output, and some requests and replies are dropped.
4. So a measured 80 Gbps against a predicted 500 Gbps is normal: the prediction was an upper bound.
5. Defensively, the BAF still matters: it tells operators which exposed services are worth closing, while total reflector capacity decides the real attack size.

lessons.title: Headers and amplification controls
lessons.summary: Headers and fragmentation change amplification measured at the IP or link layer.
lessons.body:
The previous unit counted response payload bytes per request payload byte. This unit compares that number with the IP-packet ratio, then identifies controls at senders, reflectors and the victim’s upstream network.

Two subtleties:

**Headers dilute the factor.** A UDP datagram carried in one IPv4 packet with no options has 28 bytes of IP and UDP headers (20 for IPv4, 8 for UDP); link-layer overhead is additional. The same 28 bytes are added to both the request and the response, but they are a much bigger share of a small request. So the ratio measured on whole IP packets is lower than the payload ratio, and falls most when the request is tiny. For a 40-byte request and 1,400-byte response, the payload BAF of 35 becomes about 21 at the IP-packet level:

```formula reference
BAF_IP = (B_resp + H) / (B_req + H)
where
BAF_IP: the amplification factor counting IP and UDP headers as well as payload, a plain ratio
B_resp: the response payload, in bytes
B_req: the request payload, in bytes
H: the IPv4 header (20 bytes) plus the UDP header (8 bytes), 28 bytes per packet in this unfragmented model
In words: adding the same header bytes to both sides shrinks the ratio, and shrinks it most when the request is small.
```

A full link-level ratio also needs link-layer framing and packetisation, which dilute it further.

**Packet amplification** matters too. One request producing many response packets multiplies the packets per second, which stresses routers and firewalls as well as links.

### Defending against amplification

- **Do not be a reflector**: close open resolvers, disable NTP `monlist`, never expose memcached (UDP 11211) to the internet. Memcached disabled UDP by default from version 1.5.6 after the 2018 attacks.
- **BCP 38** ingress filtering at ISPs, so spoofed packets never leave the attacker's network.
- **Protocol design**: cap amplification before validating a peer's address. QUIC permits up to three times the received UDP payload bytes before address validation; this bounds amplification rather than eliminating it.
- **Upstream scrubbing and anycast** to spread and absorb the flood.

QUIC's rule shows how protocol design can bound amplification: until a server has confirmed the client can receive at its claimed address, it may send at most three times the bytes it has received. Clients must pad UDP datagrams that carry Initial packets to at least 1,200 bytes of payload, so even the first flight gives the server some room. If the server's handshake (for example a long certificate chain) needs more, it must wait for more client bytes or validate the address first, for example with a Retry token.

## Key takeaways
- Headers and fragmentation change amplification measured at the IP or link layer.
- Source validation and closing reflectors reduce the available attack paths.
- QUIC bounds pre-validation amplification; it does not eliminate amplification.

## Further reading
- [RFC 2827 (BCP 38): Network Ingress Filtering](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2827)
- [RFC 9000: QUIC, section 8 (address validation)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000#section-8)
- [UDP-Based Amplification Attacks — CISA](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2014/01/17/udp-based-amplification-attacks)

questions.prompt: Two reflectors both have a payload bandwidth amplification factor of 30. Reflector A answers a 10-byte request payload with a 300-byte payload. Reflector B answers a 100-byte request payload with a 3,000-byte payload. Each request and response is one unfragmented IPv4/UDP packet carrying 28 bytes of headers. Measured on whole IP packets, which reflector amplifies more?

options.text: Both the same, because their payload ratios are equal
options.explanation: The header bytes are the same 28 on every packet, but they are a much larger share of A's tiny request than of B's. Equal payload ratios therefore give different IP-packet ratios.

options.text: Reflector A, because its request is smaller
options.explanation: A small request is cheap to send, but the fixed 28 header bytes nearly quadruple A's 10-byte request while barely changing its response, so A's IP-packet ratio falls the most.

options.text: Reflector B, because the fixed headers dilute its larger request far less
options.explanation: Correct. A's 38-byte request packet brings back a 328-byte packet (about 8.6 times); B's 128-byte request packet brings back 3,028 bytes (about 24 times). Headers dilute the ratio most when the request is tiny.

options.text: Neither amplifies at the IP level, because headers cancel out
options.explanation: The headers are added to both sides, not subtracted; the ratio shrinks but stays above 1 for both reflectors.

questions.workedExample:
1. The payload ratio ignores the 20-byte IPv4 and 8-byte UDP headers that every packet carries.
2. Adding the same 28 bytes to both request and response pulls the ratio down, most strongly when the request is small.
3. Reflector A: a 10-byte request becomes a 38-byte packet; the 300-byte response becomes 328. The ratio drops from 30 to under 9.
4. Reflector B: a 100-byte request becomes 128 bytes; the 3,000-byte response becomes 3,028. The ratio drops only to about 24.
5. So for an attacker paying for whole packets, B is the better amplifier. Published BAF tables (such as Rossow's) usually report payload ratios, so say which bytes you are counting. Link-layer framing would dilute both ratios further.

questions.prompt: Which of these reduce the internet's exposure to UDP amplification attacks in general, rather than just protecting one victim? Select all that apply.

options.text: ISPs applying BCP 38 ingress filtering
options.explanation: Correct. Filtering permitted source prefixes blocks external-prefix spoofing. Finer validation is needed to prevent impersonation within an allowed prefix.

options.text: Operators closing open DNS resolvers and disabling NTP `monlist`
options.explanation: Correct. Fewer reflectors means less capacity for attackers to borrow.

options.text: The victim adding a rate limit on its own firewall
options.explanation: Incorrect. This protects (at best) one victim from smaller attacks and does nothing about reflectors or spoofing; against a volumetric flood the link is full first.

options.text: Protocols such as QUIC limiting what a server sends before the client's address is validated
options.explanation: Correct. QUIC bounds pre-validation amplification at 3× received bytes. It reduces the amplification available to an attacker; it does not remove all reflection.

options.text: Memcached disabling its UDP listener by default
options.explanation: Correct. The 1.5.6 release disables UDP by default, reducing exposure unless operators enable it. Danger also depends on reachable capacity and configuration, not BAF alone.

questions.workedExample:
Reflection amplification needs a response directed to the victim and an amplifying service.

1. Source-prefix filtering limits who can be impersonated; within-prefix spoofing can remain.
2. Closing unintended reflectors removes those endpoints from the available pool.
3. QUIC bounds pre-validation amplification at 3×, rather than reducing it to zero.

These measures reduce systemic exposure. A victim-only firewall rate limit does not remove the reflectors or the upstream bandwidth bottleneck.

questions.prompt: A QUIC server receives one client Initial datagram padded to 1,200 bytes of UDP payload from an address it has not yet validated. Its full first flight, including a long certificate chain, would be about 6,000 bytes. What does RFC 9000 require?

options.text: Send all 6,000 bytes, because QUIC packets are encrypted
options.explanation: Encryption does not prove the source address. Anyone can send an Initial with a spoofed source, so encryption is no reason to send more.

options.text: Send at most three times the bytes received from that address until it is validated, then wait for more client bytes or validate the address, for example with a Retry token
options.explanation: Correct. Before validation the server may send at most three times what it has received, here 3,600 bytes. It must wait for further client datagrams or validate the address before sending the rest.

options.text: Send nothing until the client completes a TCP handshake
options.explanation: QUIC runs over UDP and has no TCP handshake. Address validation uses QUIC's own mechanisms, such as Retry tokens and handshake progress.

options.text: Send the full flight but only once its congestion window allows it
options.explanation: The congestion window is a separate limit. The anti-amplification limit applies before address validation, and here it is the smaller one.

questions.workedExample:
1. QUIC runs over UDP, so a forged Initial from a victim's address is possible.
2. A server whose first flight is much larger than the client's datagram could otherwise be an amplifier.
3. RFC 9000 section 8: until the client's address is validated, the server must not send more than three times the bytes it has received from that address. One 1,200-byte datagram allows about 3,600 bytes.
4. Clients must pad datagrams carrying Initial packets to at least 1,200 bytes, which raises the cost of each forged probe and gives honest clients a usable allowance.
5. To send the remaining data the server waits for further client datagrams (which raise the allowance) or validates the address, for example by sending a Retry and receiving the token back. Sending a Retry by itself proves nothing; only the returned token does.

The limit bounds amplification to threefold rather than removing it.

lessons.title: Packet policy and rule order
lessons.summary: A first-match filter stops at its first matching rule.
lessons.body:
The earlier threat units showed why receiving a packet does not, by itself, establish a trustworthy identity. A **firewall** is the first answer to that: a device or piece of software that sits on a boundary and decides, packet by packet or connection by connection, what is allowed through.

The second answer is to have more boundaries. **Network segmentation** splits a network into zones so that a compromise in one zone does not hand over all of them. The third answer, **zero trust**, says that network location alone never grants implicit trust.

This unit focuses on rule matching and its default policy.

## What a firewall decides on

Every firewall matches traffic against a list of **firewall rules**. The more of the packet it understands, the more precise the rules can be:

| Type | Looks at | Example rule |
|---|---|---|
| Stateless filter | Headers of one packet | Drop TCP to port 23 |
| Stateful | Headers plus connection state | Allow replies to my requests |
| Application (L7) | Protocol content | Block HTTP `POST /admin` |

Most rules are written in terms of the **5-tuple**: protocol, source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port. Add the direction (inbound or outbound) and the interface, and you can express most network policy.

### Rule order and default policy

The toy filter below uses **top-to-bottom, first-match evaluation**. Real products differ: AWS security groups combine allow rules, while nftables can continue across chains after an accept verdict. Anything that matches no rule gets **the default policy**, which should be *deny*.

```python
from ipaddress import ip_address, ip_network

RULES = [  # proto, port, source, action
    ("tcp", 22, "10.0.0.0/8", "allow"),
    ("tcp", 443, "0.0.0.0/0", "allow"),
    ("tcp", 22, "0.0.0.0/0", "deny"),
]

def check(proto, port, src):
    addr = ip_address(src)
    # Keep rule order: the first match wins.
    for p, dport, net, action in RULES:
        if p != proto or dport != port:
            # Skip a different service.
            continue
        if addr in ip_network(net):
            return action  # first match
    # No rule matched this packet.
    return "deny"  # default policy

# Compare internal SSH, public SSH and DNS.
print(check("tcp", 22, "10.1.2.3"))
print(check("tcp", 22, "203.0.113.9"))
print(check("udp", 53, "10.1.2.3"))
```

This prints `allow`, `deny`, `deny`. SSH from inside `10.0.0.0/8` matches rule 1. SSH from the internet skips rule 1 and hits rule 3. DNS matches nothing and falls through to the default.

Swap rules 1 and 3 and internal SSH breaks too, because the broad deny now matches first. Order bugs and broad rules that shadow narrow ones can contradict the intended policy. Good tooling flags **shadowed rules** that can never match.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a door supervisor's ordered checklist
> A door supervisor works down a written list and acts on the first line that fits each guest: "staff with a badge: let in", "anyone in football shirts: refuse", "ticket holders: let in". Anyone the list does not mention is refused.
>
> **How it maps:** Each line is a firewall rule, acting on the first line that fits is first-match evaluation, and "refuse anyone not mentioned" is a default-deny policy. If "refuse football shirts" sits above "staff with a badge", a staff member in a football shirt is turned away: the broad rule shadows the narrower one beneath it.
>
> **Where it stops:** A person can use judgement when the list seems wrong; a firewall applies the rules exactly. Real products also differ in how they evaluate rules: AWS security groups have no order at all, and nftables can pass a packet through several chains.

> [!tip] Default deny, both ways
> Explicit inbound and outbound allowlists can reduce exposure. Egress restrictions can obstruct some command-and-control and exfiltration paths, but allowed services may still be abused; default-deny adoption is not universal.

## Key takeaways
- A first-match filter stops at its first matching rule.
- A broad earlier rule can shadow a later specific rule.
- Explicit defaults and outbound controls make permitted paths easier to review.

## Further reading
- [Firewall (computing) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firewall_(computing))
- [Control subnet traffic with network ACLs — AWS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-network-acls.html)
- [Simple ruleset for a workstation — nftables wiki](https://wiki.nftables.org/wiki-nftables/index.php/Simple_ruleset_for_a_workstation)

questions.prompt:
A first-match firewall has these rules, then a default policy of deny:

```
1 allow tcp 443 from any
2 deny  tcp any from 198.51.100.0/24
3 allow tcp 22  from any
```

What happens to SSH (TCP 22) from 198.51.100.7, and to HTTPS from the same address?

options.text: SSH denied, HTTPS allowed
options.explanation: Correct. HTTPS matches rule 1 first and is allowed before rule 2 is reached. SSH skips rule 1, matches rule 2 and is denied.

options.text: Both denied
options.explanation: This assumes the deny for that subnet applies to everything, but rule 1 matches HTTPS first and first match wins.

options.text: Both allowed
options.explanation: SSH does not match rule 1 (wrong port), so rule 2 is reached and denies it before rule 3.

options.text: SSH allowed, HTTPS denied
options.explanation: This reads the rules from last to first. First-match evaluation goes top to bottom.

questions.workedExample:
Walk each packet down the list and stop at the first match.

**HTTPS from 198.51.100.7:**
1. Rule 1: tcp 443 from any. Match. **Allow.** Stop.

**SSH from 198.51.100.7:**
1. Rule 1: port 443? No.
2. Rule 2: tcp any from 198.51.100.0/24? Yes. **Deny.** Stop.
3. Rule 3 is never reached.

If the intent was to block that subnet entirely, rule 2 must move above rule 1.

questions.prompt:
Your firewall review tool flags rule 3 below as **shadowed**. Why?

```
1 allow tcp 80,443 from any
2 deny  tcp any    from 0.0.0.0/0
3 allow tcp 8443   from 10.0.0.0/8
```

options.text: Rule 3 is too narrow to ever be useful
options.explanation: Narrow rules are good. The issue is that it can never be reached.

options.text: Rule 3 is redundant because rule 1 already allows port 8443
options.explanation: Rule 1 covers only 80 and 443, not 8443.

options.text: Every packet rule 3 would match has already matched rule 2, so rule 3 can never take effect
options.explanation: Correct. TCP to 8443 from 10.0.0.0/8 is a subset of "TCP to any port from anywhere", which rule 2 denies first. The intended internal access is silently blocked.

options.text: Rule 3 conflicts with the default policy
options.explanation: The default policy only applies when no rule matches; here rule 2 matches first.

questions.workedExample:
1. A rule is **shadowed** when an earlier rule matches every packet it could match.
2. Rule 3 matches: TCP, port 8443, source in 10.0.0.0/8.
3. Rule 2 matches: TCP, any port, any source. That is a superset.
4. So any packet that could reach rule 3 is denied by rule 2 first.
5. Fix: move rule 3 above rule 2. With first-match semantics, put specific rules above broad ones.

lessons.title: Connection state and cloud return traffic
lessons.summary: Connection state lets policy recognise reply traffic but consumes finite memory.
lessons.body:
Rule order is only part of a firewall’s behaviour. A packet may be a reply in an existing flow, or a new attempt requiring another state entry. This unit follows that distinction into AWS subnet and interface controls.

## Stateless versus stateful

A **stateless** filter judges each packet alone. That causes a problem with replies. When your web server at port 443 answers a client, the reply goes *to* the client's **ephemeral port**, some random number such as 51,812. A stateless filter needs a rule covering the intended return traffic. For clients anywhere on the internet this often includes a range of destination ephemeral ports; source ports, addresses and protocol flags may further constrain a rule, but do not prove connection state.

A **stateful** firewall keeps **a connection table**. When it sees an allowed outbound SYN, it records the flow. Connection tracking supplies state that filtering rules can match. A known flow is accepted only when the applicable policy permits it:

```
 conntrack table (simplified)
 proto src:port        dst:port   state
 tcp   10.0.0.5:51812  1.2.3.4:443  ESTAB
 udp   10.0.0.5:40001  9.9.9.9:53   REPLIED
```

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a receptionist's log of expected replies
> A receptionist who only reads each envelope must decide from the envelope alone whether to accept it, so a rule like "accept anything addressed to the post room" lets in unexpected mail too. A receptionist who keeps a log of outgoing letters can accept a reply because it matches a letter that was sent, and can turn away mail that matches nothing.
>
> **How it maps:** The envelope-only receptionist is a stateless filter that needs broad return rules, such as allowing every ephemeral port. The log is the connection table: an allowed outbound request creates an entry, and replies that match it can be accepted by an established-traffic rule.
>
> **Where it stops:** The log takes memory and entries expire, so a flood of fake new requests can fill it and idle connections can be forgotten. Matching an entry also proves nothing about who really sent a packet; it only shows that the addresses, ports and state fit an existing flow.

On Linux this is **conntrack**. This abbreviated nftables input-chain example explicitly accepts established and related traffic:

```nftables
table inet filter {
  chain input {
    type filter hook input priority 0;
    policy drop;
    ct state established,related accept
    ct state invalid drop
    iif "lo" accept
    tcp dport 22 ip saddr 10.0.0.0/8 accept
    tcp dport { 80, 443 } accept
  }
}
```

The `inet` family covers both IPv4 and IPv6; the `ip saddr` condition is specifically IPv4. A new IPv6 SSH attempt matches neither the IPv4 SSH allow rule nor the web-port rules and falls through to drop.

This is an input-chain fragment, not a complete deployment ruleset: it omits IPv6 neighbour discovery, router advertisements, other required ICMP handling, and forwarding and outbound policy. Blindly applying it can break connectivity. UDP and ICMP tracking uses protocol-specific tuples and timeouts; a UDP reply does not establish application-level authentication.

### The cost of state

State is memory, and memory can run out. The connection table is itself a DoS target: a SYN flood or many short UDP flows can fill it, after which the firewall drops new connections, including legitimate ones. Timeouts matter too. Linux keeps an idle established TCP entry for five days by default, while many cloud load balancers and NAT gateways drop idle flows after minutes, which is why long-lived idle connections mysteriously die unless they send keepalives.

## Firewalls in the cloud

AWS is a good case study because it gives you both kinds side by side:

| | Security group | Network ACL |
|---|---|---|
| Applies to | Network interface | Subnet |
| State | Stateful | Stateless |
| Rules | Allow only | Allow and deny |
| Evaluation | All rules together | Numbered order, first match |

Because NACLs are stateless, you must explicitly allow return traffic to ephemeral ports (AWS suggests 1024 to 65535). Forgetting the outbound ephemeral rule is a classic cause of "the security group is open but nothing works".

Security groups can also reference *other security groups*: "allow port 5432 from members of `sg-web`". Within supported AWS connectivity arrangements, the reference resolves to associated interfaces' private addresses and updates automatically as interfaces join or leave the group. It is a network policy reference, not cryptographic proof of application identity; traffic through a middlebox can require different rules.

## Key takeaways
- Connection state lets policy recognise reply traffic but consumes finite memory.
- AWS security groups combine stateful allow rules; NACLs are ordered and stateless.
- Return ports and idle timeouts matter even when the service port is open.

## Further reading
- [Control traffic to resources using security groups — AWS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-security-groups.html)
- [Control subnet traffic with network ACLs — AWS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-network-acls.html)
- [Simple ruleset for a workstation — nftables wiki](https://wiki.nftables.org/wiki-nftables/index.php/Simple_ruleset_for_a_workstation)
- [Troubleshoot NAT gateways — AWS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/nat-gateway-troubleshooting.html)

questions.prompt: What does a stateful firewall track that a stateless packet filter does not?

options.text: The application data inside each packet
options.explanation: Inspecting content is what application-layer firewalls and WAFs do. Stateful tracking is about connections, not payloads.

options.text: The user who sent each packet
options.explanation: User identity is a feature of NGFWs and identity-aware proxies, not of basic stateful filtering.

options.text: Which flows are in progress, allowing rules to match connection state
options.explanation: Correct. State provides context for policy. An established/related accept rule can permit return traffic without a separate port-range rule, but tracking alone does not bypass filtering.

options.text: The physical port each packet arrived on
options.explanation: Even stateless filters can match on the interface; that is not what state means.

questions.workedExample:
1. Stateless: each packet is judged in isolation against the rules.
2. Stateful: on the first allowed packet (say an outbound SYN), the firewall records the flow: protocol, addresses, ports, state.
3. Later packets may match established or related state. Whether they are accepted depends on the applicable rules; not every recorded packet is established.
4. That is why the nftables ruleset starts with `ct state established,related accept`.

questions.prompt: An EC2 web server's security group allows inbound TCP 443 from anywhere. Its subnet's custom network ACL allows inbound TCP 443 and outbound TCP 443, and nothing else (the final rule denies everything). Clients cannot load the site. Why?

options.text: Security groups are stateless, so replies need their own rule
options.explanation: Security groups are stateful; replies to allowed inbound traffic are automatic at that layer.

options.text: The NACL is stateless, and replies go to clients' ephemeral ports, not to 443, so they are denied outbound
options.explanation: Correct. The server replies from 443 to ports such as 51,812. The NACL has no outbound rule for those ports. Add an outbound allow for TCP 1024–65535.

options.text: NACL rules are ignored when a security group exists
options.explanation: Both apply: traffic must pass the subnet's NACL and the interface's security group.

options.text: The NACL must also allow inbound ephemeral ports for the requests to arrive
options.explanation: The requests arrive on port 443, which is allowed. It is the outbound replies to ephemeral ports that fail.

questions.workedExample:
Trace one connection from client port 51812:

```
in : client:51812 -> srv:443
     NACL in 443   allow
     SG   in 443   allow
out: srv:443 -> client:51812
     SG   stateful, allow
     NACL out 51812? no rule
     -> DENY
```

The NACL judges the reply as a fresh packet with destination port 51,812. Fix: outbound NACL rule allowing TCP 1024–65535 to 0.0.0.0/0.

questions.prompt: Which statements about AWS security groups and network ACLs are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Security groups support only allow rules
options.explanation: Correct. Security groups have no explicit deny rules. For traffic they filter, unmatched new traffic is denied; documented exceptions such as Amazon-provided DNS are not blocked by security groups.

options.text: Network ACL rules are evaluated in number order, and the first match applies
options.explanation: Correct. That is why rule numbering (100, 200, ...) leaves gaps for inserting rules later.

options.text: Security group rules are evaluated in the order they were created
options.explanation: Incorrect. All security group rules are evaluated together; since they are all allows, order cannot matter.

options.text: A security group rule can allow traffic from members of another security group
options.explanation: Correct within supported AWS arrangements. A source-group reference permits traffic from associated interfaces' private addresses; middlebox routing and connectivity restrictions matter.

options.text: Network ACLs apply to individual network interfaces
