lessons.title: IDS placement and signature meaning
lessons.summary: Passive IDS sensors analyse a copy; inline IPS devices can block traffic.
lessons.body:
The earlier units focused on preventive controls. Prevention can fail: a password is phished, a VPN appliance is unpatched, a firewall rule is too broad. The question then is how quickly you notice. **Dwell time** is the interval from intrusion to detection.

Detection on the network rests on three kinds of evidence, which trade detail against cost:

| Source | Detail | Cost to keep |
|---|---|---|
| Packet capture | Captured packet bytes, subject to truncation and loss | Potentially high |
| Protocol logs (Zeek) | Selected connection, protocol-exchange or file events | Depends on logging |
| Flow records | Aggregated traffic sharing selected attributes | Depends on export |

On top of the evidence sit detection systems that raise alerts. This unit introduces alerting engines; the following units examine alert precision and the evidence those engines consume.

## IDS and IPS

An **intrusion detection system** (IDS) watches traffic and raises alerts. An **intrusion prevention system** (IPS) sits inline and can also drop traffic.

```
 IDS (passive):
 net ---+---> switch ---> LAN
        | SPAN/TAP copy
        v
      [IDS] --> alerts

 IPS (inline):
 net ---> [IPS] ---> LAN
            |
       drop or pass
```

- An IDS is fed a copy of traffic from a switch **SPAN** (mirror) port or a network **TAP**, or in the cloud via traffic mirroring. A passive sensor is outside the forwarding path; automatic response integrations can still affect traffic. A mirror can lose packets when the copied traffic exceeds its monitoring-port capacity.
- An IPS can stop an attack in progress, but it adds latency and becomes a point of failure. You must choose **fail-open** (traffic flows if the IPS dies, unprotected) or **fail-closed** (the network goes down with it). A false positive on a blocking rule can disrupt legitimate traffic; alert-only rules do not themselves block it.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a CCTV room and a door supervisor
> A shop can watch its entrance on CCTV from a back room, or post a supervisor at the door. The CCTV operator sees a copy of everything and can raise the alarm, but cannot stop anyone directly; if the camera feed drops out, the shop stays open. The supervisor can turn people away, but every customer queues past them, and if the supervisor leaves the door has to be either locked or left unguarded.
>
> **How it maps:** The CCTV room is a passive IDS fed from a SPAN port or TAP: it analyses a copy of the traffic and raises alerts. The door supervisor is an inline IPS: it can drop traffic, adds delay and is a point of failure. Locking or leaving the door when the supervisor is absent is the fail-closed or fail-open choice. Turning away a regular customer by mistake is a false positive on a blocking rule.
>
> **Where it stops:** A camera feed shows everything in view, but a mirror port can silently lose packets under load and encrypted traffic hides its contents from both devices. A passive sensor can also trigger automated responses elsewhere, so "only watching" is not always harmless.

Network IDS (NIDS) watch the wire; host IDS (HIDS) and EDR agents watch processes and files on each machine. They complement each other: hosts see what happened inside encrypted sessions, networks see machines that have no agent, such as printers, cameras and anything the attacker brought.

### Signatures and anomalies

**Signature-based** detection matches known patterns. Snort and Suricata are examples of open-source engines. A Suricata rule (backslashes continue a rule across lines):

```suricata
alert http any any -> $HOME_NET any ( \
  msg:"SQLi attempt in URI"; \
  flow:established,to_server; \
  http.uri; content:"union select"; \
  nocase; \
  classtype:web-application-attack; \
  sid:1000001; rev:1;)
```

The header (`alert http any any -> $HOME_NET any`) says what traffic to consider; the options say what to look for. `flow:established,to_server` selects traffic towards the server in a flow the engine considers established. This is connection tracking, not cryptographic peer authentication or a guarantee against forged traffic; midstream handling also depends on configuration. `http.uri` selects the normalised URI buffer. The string match is only a teaching example, not a complete SQL-injection detector.

Signatures match specified patterns, which can occur in both known and previously unseen attacks, or in benign traffic. **Anomaly-based** detection learns a baseline (normal hosts, ports, volumes and times) and alerts on deviations: a workstation suddenly talking SMB to fifty others, a server uploading gigabytes at 3 a.m. It can flag previously unseen behaviour, but deviations can be legitimate. Relative false-positive rates depend on the detector, data and threshold.

## Key takeaways
- Passive IDS sensors analyse a copy; inline IPS devices can block traffic.
- Inline failure policy trades continued connectivity against unfiltered passage.
- An established flow is connection state, not cryptographic sender authentication.

## Further reading
- [Intrusion detection system — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intrusion_detection_system)
- [Suricata rules format — Suricata docs](https://docs.suricata.io/en/latest/rules/intro.html)
- [Zeek documentation](https://docs.zeek.org/en/v7.1.1/logs/index.html)

questions.prompt: What is the key operational difference between an IDS fed from a SPAN port and an inline IPS?

options.text: An IDS can decrypt TLS and an IPS cannot
options.explanation: Neither can decrypt TLS without keys or interception; this is unrelated to the deployment mode.

options.text: An inline IPS can block traffic and affect forwarding; a passive SPAN-fed IDS observes a copy and raises alerts
options.explanation: Correct. Inline placement gives the power to block and the risk of blocking, plus the fail-open versus fail-closed decision.

options.text: An IDS uses signatures and an IPS uses anomaly detection
options.explanation: Both can use either technique; Suricata runs as either an IDS or an IPS.

options.text: An IPS needs no tuning because it blocks automatically
options.explanation: Blocking rules need careful tuning because false positives can disrupt legitimate traffic; alert-only rules do not themselves block.

questions.workedExample: A passive IDS is outside the forwarding path. An IPS can drop traffic, adding latency and a failure mode governed by fail-open or fail-closed design. False positives on blocking rules can disrupt users. An IDS connected to automated response systems can also cause traffic changes, so passive placement alone does not make all integrations harmless.

questions.prompt: A Suricata rule includes `flow:established,to_server;`. What does this option achieve?

options.text: It makes the rule match only on traffic from the server to the client
options.explanation: `to_server` means client-to-server direction.

options.text: It blocks the connection when the rule matches
options.explanation: Blocking comes from the action (`drop` in IPS mode), not from `flow`.

options.text: It establishes a TCP connection to the server to test it
options.explanation: Suricata is passive here; it does not create connections.

options.text: It restricts matching to traffic towards the server in a flow that the engine considers established
options.explanation: Correct. Flow state and direction constrain matching; they do not cryptographically authenticate the sender or guarantee resistance to forged traffic.

questions.workedExample: For ordinary tracked TCP, established state follows the handshake; midstream pickup can alter what was observed. The to_server direction excludes server-to-client responses. For other protocols, established state can have another meaning, such as observing both directions. This is a matching constraint, not a claim that excluded traffic cannot be an attack.

lessons.title: Why a rare attack creates many false alerts
lessons.summary: Alert precision depends on attack prevalence as well as detector sensitivity.
lessons.body:
A detector with a small false-positive rate can still create a large investigation workload. The denominator matters: rare malicious events may be outnumbered by benign events by many orders of magnitude.

### The base-rate problem

Even a small false-positive rate can overwhelm true alerts when malicious events are rare. The question an analyst cares about is: when an alert fires, how likely is it to be real? That fraction is the detector's **alert precision**. It depends on how common attacks are (the **base rate**) as well as on the detector, because the false alerts come from the huge pool of benign events while the true alerts come from the tiny pool of malicious ones.

Consider a network that sees 10,000,000 connections a day, of which 100 are malicious. A detector catches 99 % of attacks and wrongly flags only 0.1 % of benign connections. On a typical day you would expect:

| Alerts | Expected per day |
|---|---|
| Real attacks caught (99 % of 100) | about 99 |
| Benign connections flagged (0.1 % of 9,999,900) | about 10,000 |
| Share of alerts that are real | about 1 % |

So roughly 99 of every 100 alerts are false, even though the detector sounds excellent on paper. Nothing is broken: benign connections outnumber attacks 100,000 to one, so a tiny false-positive rate still produces far more false alerts than there are attacks to find. That workload can make triage difficult; it does not prove that every analyst will miss the true alerts.

The same reasoning predicts which changes help. Catching 100 % of attacks instead of 99 % adds about one real alert and leaves precision near 1 %. Cutting the false-positive rate tenfold, to 0.01 %, leaves about 1,000 false alerts and lifts precision to about 9 %. A higher base rate would also raise precision, which is why the same rule can be useful on a small, high-risk network segment and useless across a whole network.

```formula reference
precision = tp / (tp + (1 − p)f)
where
precision: the fraction of alerts that are real attacks, from 0 to 1 (also called positive predictive value)
p: prevalence (the base rate): the fraction of all events that are malicious
t: sensitivity (true-positive rate): the fraction of malicious events the detector flags
f: false-positive rate: the fraction of benign events the detector wrongly flags
In words: real alerts are the detected share of the rare malicious events; false alerts are the wrongly flagged share of the much larger number of benign events; precision is real alerts divided by all alerts, so when attacks are rare the false-positive rate dominates.
```

This is Bayes' theorem applied to alerts. The counts above are expected values under constant rates, not guaranteed daily outcomes, and precision is undefined if the detector never alerts.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: screening everyone for a rare illness
> A clinic screens 10,000 healthy-looking people for an illness that only one of them has. Even a test that is wrong for just 1 in 1,000 healthy people will flag about ten of them, so a positive result is far more likely to be a false alarm than a real case.
>
> **How it maps:** The people screened are network connections, the illness is an attack, the test's false-alarm rate on healthy people is the detector's false-positive rate, and the chance that a positive result is real is alert precision. Screening a high-risk group instead, where the illness is common, is like applying a rule only where attacks are likely.
>
> **Where it stops:** Patients do not change their symptoms to fool the test, but attackers deliberately make malicious traffic look benign, and network traffic is not a set of independent cases with fixed rates. Real rates must be measured in your own environment.

This is why mature teams tune aggressively, suppress noisy rules, correlate network alerts with host and identity signals in a SIEM, and measure precision in their own environment. Malware-domain and honeypot alerts can be useful, but shared infrastructure, research traffic and mistakes can still create false positives.

## Key takeaways
- Alert precision depends on attack prevalence as well as detector sensitivity.
- Cutting false positives raises precision far more than catching the last few attacks.
- The worked counts are expected values, not guaranteed daily outcomes.
- Tune and correlate evidence using the actual operating environment.

## Further reading
- [Base rate fallacy — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Base_rate_fallacy)
- [Positive and negative predictive values — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Positive_and_negative_predictive_values)

questions.prompt: A detector tested at 99% sensitivity and a 0.1% false-positive rate is deployed on a network with about 10,000,000 connections a day, roughly 100 of them malicious. Analysts complain that about 99 of every 100 alerts are false and say the detector must be faulty. What best explains this, and which change would raise the share of real alerts the most?

options.text: The detector is faulty, because with 99% sensitivity at least 99% of its alerts should be real attacks
options.explanation: This confuses sensitivity (the share of attacks that are caught) with precision (the share of alerts that are real). A detector can catch 99% of attacks and still produce mostly false alerts when attacks are rare.

options.text: Nothing is broken: benign connections vastly outnumber attacks, so even 0.1% of them swamps the real alerts; cutting false positives helps most
options.explanation: Correct. About 99 real alerts compete with about 10,000 false ones. Cutting the false-positive rate tenfold, for example by tuning rules or correlating with host and identity signals, leaves about 1,000 false alerts and lifts precision from about 1% to about 9%.

options.text: Raise sensitivity to 100% so that every attack is caught and the real alerts dominate
options.explanation: That adds about one real alert a day. The false alerts from roughly ten million benign connections are unchanged, so precision stays near 1%.

options.text: Hire more analysts so that every alert is investigated, which raises the share that are real
options.explanation: More analysts can handle the workload, but the share of alerts that are real is a property of the detector and the traffic. It stays at about 1%.

questions.workedExample:
1. Separate two different questions. Sensitivity asks: of the attacks, how many are caught? Precision asks: of the alerts, how many are real?
2. Real alerts come from the small pool of attacks: about 99% of 100, so about 99 a day.
3. False alerts come from the huge pool of benign connections: 0.1% of nearly 10 million, so about 10,000 a day.
4. So only about 1 alert in 100 is real. The detector is behaving exactly as tested; the rarity of attacks (the base rate) is the cause.
5. The lever that matters is the false-positive rate, because it multiplies the largest number. A tenfold cut gives about 99 real against about 1,000 false alerts, roughly 9% precision. Catching the last 1% of attacks or adding staff barely changes precision.
6. In practice teams tune or suppress noisy rules, restrict rules to where attacks are likely, and correlate network alerts with host and identity evidence before raising them.

lessons.title: Capture filters, display filters and TCP flags
lessons.summary: tcpdump capture filters and Wireshark display filters use different syntax.
lessons.body:
Packet captures preserve observations at one point in a path. This unit shows how to choose packets and read TCP flag output without confusing a reset, silence or a heuristic retransmission label with a complete diagnosis.

## Packet capture with tcpdump

When you need ground truth, capture packets. `tcpdump` uses **BPF capture filters**. On supported live-capture platforms filtering can run in the kernel; offline capture-file filtering runs in userspace:

```sh
# 20 packets to or from one host, no DNS
# or port-name lookups
tcpdump -i eth0 -nn -c 20 host 10.0.0.5

# request the maximum snapshot length
tcpdump -i eth0 -nn -s 0 \
  -w web.pcap 'tcp port 443'

# IPv4 SYN set, ACK clear
tcpdump -nn \
  'tcp[tcpflags] & (tcp-syn|tcp-ack)
     == tcp-syn'

# ring buffer: 10 files of 100 MB
tcpdump -i eth0 -w ring.pcap -C 100 -W 10
```

`-nn` matters on a busy box: name resolution can add delay and generate DNS traffic. Cached results and local host databases mean this is not necessarily a DNS query for every address. A line of output looks like this (wrapped to fit):

```
12:00:01.000123 IP 10.0.0.5.51812 >
  203.0.113.10.443: Flags [S],
  seq 3021930120, win 64240, length 0
```

The flags are the quickest way to read a conversation:

| Flags | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `[S]` | SYN, opening |
| `[S.]` | SYN-ACK |
| `[.]` | ACK flag; payload may still be present |
| `[P.]` | PSH and ACK flags; inspect length for payload |
| `[F.]` | FIN, closing |
| `[R]` | RST, refused or aborted |

SYNs to many ports can indicate a scan, but may also be authorised diagnostics. A reset indicates active rejection or abort somewhere along the path, possibly by a middlebox. Silence could reflect filtering, loss, an unavailable host or replies travelling by a path the sensor cannot see; it does not identify a firewall by itself.

### Wireshark

Wireshark decodes hundreds of protocols and is the tool for understanding a capture. Its **display filters** use a different syntax from BPF capture filters, a constant source of confusion:

| Capture (libpcap) | Display (Wireshark) |
|---|---|
| `tcp port 80` | `tcp.port == 80` |
| `host 10.0.0.5` | `ip.addr == 10.0.0.5` |

Useful display filters for investigations:

- `tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0`: connection attempts.
- `tcp.analysis.retransmission`: packets Wireshark heuristically classifies as retransmissions; investigate capture loss and reordering before inferring network loss.
- `dns.flags.rcode == 3`: NXDOMAIN answers. Bursts of random-looking names can indicate malware using domain-generation algorithms.
- `tls.handshake.type == 1`: visible ClientHellos; ECH can hide the real server name in the encrypted inner ClientHello.

"Follow TCP Stream" reassembles a conversation. For TLS you can decrypt your *own* captures if the client writes its session secrets to a file: browsers and many libraries honour the `SSLKEYLOGFILE` environment variable, and Wireshark reads it.

## Key takeaways
- tcpdump capture filters and Wireshark display filters use different syntax.
- Flags and lengths describe packet observations rather than proving intent.
- Name-resolution controls, capture loss and TCP stream reconstruction context affect interpretation.

## Further reading
- [tcpdump and libpcap](https://www.tcpdump.org/)
- [Wireshark display filters — Wireshark wiki](https://wiki.wireshark.org/DisplayFilters)

questions.prompt: In tcpdump output, a client sends `Flags [S]` to a server's port 8080 and immediately receives `Flags [R.]`. What does that tell you?

options.text: The connection was established and then reset by the application
options.explanation: A connection never got established: there was no SYN-ACK.

options.text: A firewall silently dropped the SYN
options.explanation: A silent drop produces no reply at all; here something answered with a reset.

options.text: The server sent data and closed normally
options.explanation: FIN indicates an orderly TCP close. PSH is not required for data; inspect payload length rather than inferring data solely from flags.

options.text: Something returned a reset, actively rejecting the attempt; it may be the destination host or a middlebox
options.explanation: A reset in response to SYN indicates rejection. It does not prove the destination host was reached or which device generated the response.

questions.workedExample: SYN followed by SYN-ACK indicates willingness to establish TCP. SYN followed by RST-ACK indicates active rejection, potentially by a middlebox. No observed reply could mean filtering, packet loss, an unavailable host or replies travelling by a path the observer cannot see. These observations alone do not locate the failure or prove the actual destination port state.

questions.prompt: What does `tcpdump -nn` change, and why can that help on a busy server?

options.text: It disables address and port-name resolution, avoiding associated lookup delays and possible DNS traffic
options.explanation: Name resolution can add work and traffic, but caches and local databases mean not every address necessarily generates a DNS query.

options.text: It captures full-size packets instead of truncating them
options.explanation: Snapshot length is controlled with -s. The value 0 requests the implementation maximum, which is still finite.

options.text: It enables promiscuous mode
options.explanation: Promiscuous mode is a different setting of the capture interface. The -p option asks tcpdump not to request it; -nn affects displayed names.

options.text: It writes packets to a file
options.explanation: That is `-w file.pcap`.

questions.workedExample: Numeric output such as 10.0.0.5.443 avoids resolving addresses and service names. Without -nn, resolution may use local databases, cached results or DNS; DNS queries can themselves appear in captures. Disabling these lookups can reduce output delays, but it does not guarantee that a busy capture loses no packets.

questions.prompt: An engineer types `tcp.port == 443` into tcpdump's filter and gets a syntax error, then types `tcp port 443` into Wireshark's display-filter bar and gets an error there too. What is going on?

options.text: Both tools are broken and need reinstalling
options.explanation: These are expected errors from using one tool's syntax in the other.

options.text: Port 443 cannot be filtered because it is encrypted
options.explanation: TLS encrypts application content, not the enclosing TCP ports. Port filtering works when the relevant header is present and supported; later fragments and encapsulation can limit visibility.

options.text: tcpdump uses BPF capture-filter syntax (`tcp port 443`); Wireshark's display filters use field syntax (`tcp.port == 443`)
options.explanation: Correct. Wireshark's *capture* filter box also uses BPF; its *display* filter bar uses its own language.

options.text: Wireshark only supports UDP display filters
options.explanation: Wireshark display filters support TCP and hundreds of other protocols.

questions.workedExample:
| Where | Syntax | Example |
|---|---|---|
| tcpdump | capture syntax | `tcp port 443` |
| Wireshark capture | capture syntax | `tcp port 443` |
| Wireshark display | fields | `tcp.port == 443` |

1. Live capture filters can run in the kernel on supported platforms; offline filtering runs in userspace.
2. Display filters inspect fields exposed by Wireshark dissectors, such as `tls.handshake.type == 1`. Encrypted or unsupported fields may be unavailable.
3. Use the correct language for each input box; punctuation alone is not a reliable syntax test.

lessons.title: Capture artefacts and storage budgets
lessons.summary: Host offloads can expose large buffers and incomplete checksums before wire transmission.
lessons.body:
A packet capture is shaped by its observation point and retention settings. Before diagnosing impossible packet sizes or promising a month of retention, separate host-buffer artefacts from bytes actually stored.

> [!warning] Capture pitfalls
> - **Offloads.** Depending on the capture hook and enabled offloads, host captures can show large buffers before transmit segmentation or after receive coalescing, and outbound checksums before hardware fills them in. Such apparent errors need not occur on the wire.
> - **Drops.** A busy capture can drop packets; tcpdump reports "dropped by kernel" on exit.
> - **Storage.** Full capture fills disks quickly (worked out below). A physical link rate is not identical to recorded packet bytes, because link-layer framing and gaps also consume capacity. Choose retention from measured volume and budget.
> - **Privacy and law.** Captures contain personal data and credentials; handle them as sensitive.

### How much storage does full capture need?

Storage grows in direct proportion to both the recorded rate and the retention time: double either and you double the disk. Remember to divide a bit rate by 8 to get bytes. Recording packet bytes at a steady 1 Gbps writes 125 megabytes every second, which is about 10.8 terabytes (decimal) a day before capture-file overhead. Keeping 30 days of that needs about 324 TB; at 2 Gbps it is about 650 TB.

That is why full capture usually has short retention, often a rolling buffer of hours or days, or is triggered only when needed. Teams commonly keep much smaller evidence for longer: protocol logs and flow records summarise the same traffic at a small fraction of the size, at the cost of losing payload detail. Compression helps less than you might hope, because most web traffic is now encrypted, and encrypted bytes barely compress.

## Key takeaways
- Host offloads can expose large buffers and incomplete checksums before wire transmission.
- Capture volume uses recorded bytes, not physical link capacity alone.
- Full-capture storage scales with rate and retention; keep full packets briefly and summaries longer.

## Further reading
- [tcpdump and libpcap](https://www.tcpdump.org/)
- [Segmentation offloads — Linux kernel documentation](https://docs.kernel.org/networking/segmentation-offloads.html)
- [Wireshark display filters — Wireshark wiki](https://wiki.wireshark.org/DisplayFilters)

questions.prompt: A team must be able to investigate incidents up to 30 days old. Captured traffic on their internet link averages 2 Gbps, which is about 21.6 TB of packet bytes a day, and their evidence store holds about 100 TB. Which plan fits that budget while keeping the most useful evidence?

options.text: Keep full packet capture for all 30 days and rely on compression to close the gap
options.explanation: Thirty days at about 21.6 TB a day is roughly 650 TB, more than six times the budget. Most web traffic is now encrypted, and encrypted bytes barely compress, so compression cannot be relied on to close a gap that size.

options.text: Keep a rolling full capture of about four days, and keep flow records and protocol logs for the full 30 days
options.explanation: Correct. 100 TB holds about four and a half days of full packets. Flow records and protocol logs are far smaller, so they can cover the whole 30 days, and the recent full capture adds packet detail for fresh incidents.

options.text: Size the store from the link's 10 Gbps capacity rather than the measured average, to be safe
options.explanation: That makes the requirement five times larger, not smaller, and capture volume should be planned from recorded bytes, not the physical link rate. It does not fit a 100 TB budget.

options.text: Capture only inbound packets, which halves the storage and still covers 30 days
options.explanation: Halving 650 TB still leaves about 325 TB, over three times the budget, and dropping one direction throws away half of every conversation, including outbound exfiltration.

questions.workedExample:
1. Storage scales with rate and time: about 21.6 TB a day for 30 days is about 650 TB of full packets.
2. The budget is about 100 TB, so full capture can cover only about four to five days.
3. Compression cannot close a sixfold gap when most traffic is encrypted, and capturing one direction both falls short and loses evidence.
4. So split the evidence by cost: a short rolling buffer of full packets for detailed analysis of recent events, plus flow records and protocol logs, which are much smaller, for the full 30 days.
5. These are packet-byte figures; file overhead and replication add to them, so measure the real system before committing to a retention period.

questions.prompt: A Linux host capture shows outbound TCP buffers carrying 28,960 payload bytes with apparent bad checksums on a link with a 1,500-byte IP MTU. What is a likely explanation to investigate first?

options.text: The server is sending jumbo frames that the network will drop
options.explanation: With segmentation offload, the captured buffer can exceed the IP MTU while resulting wire IP packets respect it. Ethernet frames additionally include link-layer headers and trailers.

options.text: Segmentation and checksum offload: the kernel hands large segments to the NIC, which splits them and fills in checksums after the capture point
options.explanation: Correct as a likely offload artefact. Compare a suitable external capture and the offload configuration before concluding that malformed packets went onto the wire.

options.text: An attacker is corrupting packets
options.explanation: This pattern is consistent with offload artefacts; it does not by itself establish tampering or exclude every other cause.

options.text: The capture file is corrupt
options.explanation: A capture-file problem is possible in general, but large transmit buffers and incomplete checksums specifically suggest offload effects.

questions.workedExample:
1. On this link each full-size wire packet has room for 1,500 bytes, minus a 20-byte IPv4 header and a 32-byte TCP header (20 bytes plus 12 bytes of options such as timestamps), leaving 1,448 bytes of TCP payload.
2. The captured buffer holds 28,960 payload bytes, which is exactly 20 of those full-size segments joined together.
3. That exact multiple is a strong hint that the buffer was captured before the NIC split it. A capture before transmit offload completes can show the large buffer and unfinished checksums. Receive coalescing can cause large apparent packets at some capture hooks too. Actual visibility depends on the operating system, driver, offloads and capture point.

lessons.title: Evidence available in encrypted traffic
lessons.summary: Encrypted application payloads require appropriate keys to inspect.
lessons.body:
A passive sensor without session secrets cannot read protected application contents. It can still correlate observable traffic patterns, provided each conclusion respects what was actually captured.

## Encrypted traffic

When traffic is encrypted, a passive sensor without decryption keys cannot inspect application plaintext. Defenders lean on metadata:

- **Who talks to whom**, how often and how much. Malware **beaconing** to its command server at regular intervals shows up in timing even when encrypted.
- **Visible TLS handshake metadata**: ordinary ClientHello SNI can reveal a requested name; ECH hides the inner name while an outer public name can remain visible. TLS 1.3 encrypts certificate messages, so a passive observer without keys cannot generally read them.
- **TLS fingerprints**: features of the ClientHello can help group similar clients, but are not authenticated software identities. Different clients may share a fingerprint, and an attacker can imitate one. Changes in parameter ordering can also affect order-sensitive fingerprints.
- **DNS logs**, which can reveal names looked up through the observed resolver. Cached answers, direct IP connections and unobserved encrypted DNS create gaps.

The alternative is **TLS interception** at a proxy, which restores payload visibility at the cost of the risks described in the earlier firewall and segmentation units. Any interception policy must define which traffic it can inspect and which traffic it exempts.

**Zeek** sits in between: it parses traffic into structured logs (`conn.log`, `dns.log`, `http.log`, `ssl.log`, `files.log`) whose record units depend on the log type. These logs retain selected metadata; encrypted application contents remain unavailable without decryption. Storage and usefulness depend on the enabled analysers and traffic.

## Key takeaways
- Encrypted application payloads require appropriate keys to inspect.
- Visible names, addresses, timing and fingerprints are useful but incomplete signals.
- ECH, caching and unobserved DNS paths limit what a passive sensor can infer.

## Further reading
- [Zeek documentation](https://docs.zeek.org/en/v7.1.1/logs/index.html)
- [RFC 9849: TLS Encrypted Client Hello](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9849.html)
- [Intrusion detection system — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intrusion_detection_system)

questions.prompt: Most traffic on your network is now TLS 1.3. Which signals can a network sensor still use to detect malware without decrypting traffic? Select all that apply.

options.text: Regular beaconing intervals and sizes to the same destination
options.explanation: Correct within the observed path: encryption normally leaves packet timing and outer sizes visible, though tunnels, padding and missing observations can obscure application behaviour.

options.text: The SNI hostname in the ClientHello, where ECH is not in use
options.explanation: Correct. Without ECH, SNI is sent in clear.

options.text: JA3/JA4 fingerprints of the ClientHello
options.explanation: Correct as heuristic signals from visible ClientHello features. Fingerprints can collide or be imitated; they do not authenticate the software identity.

options.text: The HTTP URL paths requested
options.explanation: Incorrect. Paths are inside the encrypted HTTP request.

options.text: The server certificate's subject in TLS 1.3
options.explanation: Incorrect. TLS 1.3 encrypts Certificate messages. Initial certificate-based TLS 1.2 handshakes exposed them, as did earlier versions; resumed handshakes need not send certificates.

questions.workedExample:
What is still in clear with TLS 1.3 (no ECH):

| Signal | Visible? |
|---|---|
| IPs, ports, timing, sizes | Yes |
| ClientHello: SNI, ciphers, extensions | Yes |
| Certificate | No |
| HTTP method, path, headers | No |

DNS and flow logs can add evidence within their coverage. ECH conceals the real name in the inner ClientHello; an outer public name can remain visible. Resolver caches and encrypted or unobserved DNS limit name visibility. No signal is universally best.

lessons.title: Flow records and bounded scan heuristics
lessons.summary: Flow definitions, sampling and time windows vary across export systems.
lessons.body:
Flow records trade raw packet detail for selected counters and attributes. This unit uses that summary to investigate communication patterns while keeping sampling, logging gaps and legitimate scanning in view.

## Flow records

A **flow record** summarises packets grouped by selected attributes within an observation interval. Common fields include a 5-tuple, timestamps, counters and TCP flags, but templates and the rules for grouping packets into records vary. One TCP connection can produce multiple records.

- **NetFlow** (Cisco, v5 and v9) and its IETF standard successor **IPFIX** (RFC 7011): routers or probes export flow records to a collector.
- **sFlow** statistically samples packets at a configured average rate and exports sampled packet-header data plus counters. This is not necessarily a strict count such as exactly every 1,000th packet; sampled header bytes can include some payload.
- Where flow export uses **packet sampling** (for example an average of 1 in 1,000 packets), it reduces observation volume but can miss short flows and introduces uncertainty into estimates.

In AWS, **VPC Flow Logs** record traffic on network interfaces. A default-format record looks like this (shown one field per line):

```
version       2
account-id    123456789012
interface-id  eni-0a1b2c3d
srcaddr       203.0.113.9
dstaddr       10.0.1.5
srcport       40001
dstport       22
protocol      6 (TCP)
packets       1
bytes         44
start, end    epoch seconds
action        REJECT
log-status    OK
```

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: an itemised phone bill
> An itemised phone bill lists every call: which number rang which, when, for how long and whether it connected. It never records what was said. That is often enough to spot a pattern, such as one number ringing hundreds of others in a minute, but it cannot prove what any caller intended.
>
> **How it maps:** Each bill line is a flow record: the numbers are the source and destination addresses and ports, the duration and call charges are the timestamps and packet and byte counters, and "connected or not" is like the ACCEPT or REJECT action. A packet capture is the call recording, far more detailed and far bulkier.
>
> **Where it stops:** A phone bill normally lists every call, but flow exporters may sample packets, split one connection into several records, publish records only after an aggregation window, and leave documented gaps such as traffic to the Amazon-provided DNS resolver.

`action` reports ACCEPT or REJECT. A rejection can arise from security groups, NACLs or packets arriving after a connection has closed; this field alone does not identify a particular rule. They have blind spots: traffic to the Amazon-provided DNS resolver, DHCP and the instance metadata service is not logged, so DNS-based activity needs Route 53 Resolver query logs instead. The default maximum time window for each record is 10 minutes, with a 1-minute option; Nitro interfaces use at most 1 minute regardless. Publication adds delay, and SKIPDATA records disclose some logging gaps.

A simple scan detector over simplified flow records (source, destination, port, action):

```python
from collections import defaultdict

LOG = """
203.0.113.9 10.0.1.5 22 REJECT
203.0.113.9 10.0.1.5 23 REJECT
203.0.113.9 10.0.1.5 80 ACCEPT
203.0.113.9 10.0.1.5 3389 REJECT
203.0.113.9 10.0.1.6 22 REJECT
10.0.2.7 10.0.1.5 5432 ACCEPT
10.0.2.7 10.0.1.5 5432 ACCEPT
"""

targets = defaultdict(set)
rejects = defaultdict(int)
for line in LOG.strip().splitlines():
    src, dst, port, action = line.split()
    # Deduplicate destination pairs.
    targets[src].add((dst, int(port)))
    if action == "REJECT":
        # Count rejected records.
        rejects[src] += 1

for src in sorted(targets):
    n, r = len(targets[src]), rejects[src]
    # Use the example threshold.
    flag = "SCAN?" if n >= 4 else ""
    print(src, n, r, flag)
```

Ignoring the trailing space on the unflagged line, this prints `10.0.2.7 1 0` and `203.0.113.9 5 4 SCAN?`. The app server's two connections go to one `(host, port)` pair; the external address probes five pairs, mostly rejected. Real detectors add a time window, thresholds tuned to the environment and allowlists for legitimate scanners, and distinct destination pairs per source are one useful heuristic, not proof of a malicious scan.

Within its coverage, flow data can help investigate questions such as: which hosts did this compromised machine talk to? Did anything inside send unusual volumes to the internet (exfiltration)? When did this start? Retention depends on record volume, cost and policy; small individual records do not guarantee months of affordable storage.

## Putting it together

A practical network-detection stack for a medium organisation:

1. **Flow logs at relevant observation points** (budgeted retention) for investigation and anomaly detection.
2. **DNS and proxy logs** for destinations.
3. **Zeek and Suricata** at key choke points (internet edge, between major network segments).
4. **Short-retention or triggered full capture** where the detail is worth the storage.
5. Everything into a **SIEM**, correlated with host (EDR) and identity logs, with detections tuned for precision.

Segmentation (the earlier firewall and segmentation units) helps detection too: a denied connection between network segments can merit investigation, but configuration errors and legitimate discovery can also produce it.

## Key takeaways
- Flow definitions, sampling and time windows vary across export systems.
- VPC Flow Logs have documented coverage gaps and aggregation behaviour.
- Distinct destination pairs are a useful scan heuristic, not proof of malicious intent.

questions.prompt: An incident responder is using AWS VPC Flow Logs to investigate a compromised instance. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: The action field reports acceptance or rejection, but does not uniquely identify the rejecting rule
options.explanation: Correct. REJECT may reflect security-group or NACL rules, or packets arriving after a connection has closed.

options.text: Flow logs record the DNS queries the instance made to the Amazon-provided resolver
options.explanation: Incorrect. Traffic to the Amazon DNS resolver is not logged; use Route 53 Resolver query logs for that.

options.text: Records are aggregated over a capture window, so they are not real-time
options.explanation: Correct. The default maximum is 10 minutes with a 1-minute option; Nitro interfaces always use at most 1 minute. Publication adds further delay.

options.text: Flow logs contain the payload of each connection
options.explanation: Incorrect. They are metadata only: addresses, ports, protocol, counts, times, action.

options.text: Flow logs can show which external addresses the instance sent large byte counts to
options.explanation: Correct. Summing bytes by destination is a standard way to look for exfiltration.

questions.workedExample:
| Claim | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Accept/reject visible | Yes, `action` |
| DNS to Amazon resolver | Not logged |
| Real-time | No, aggregated |
| Payload | No |
| Volume by destination | Yes, `bytes` |

For one observation point and appropriate outbound-traffic records, group by destination and compare byte totals with a baseline. Account for translated addresses, duplicate observations and missing records. Large volume alone does not establish exfiltration; SKIPDATA and documented exclusions limit completeness.
